sections.title: 1. Meaning, Classifications & Core Characteristics of Part III

masteryZone.q: Which of the following categories of Fundamental Rights is described by the Supreme Court as the basic structure of the Constitution?
opts: Right to Property (Article 31)
Right to Equality (Article 14)
Right to Freedom of Religion (Article 25)
Both B and C
masteryZone.sol: Both Article 14 (Equality) and Article 25 (Freedom of Religion, reflecting Secularism) have been held by the Supreme Court as part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following statements are correct regarding the characteristics of Fundamental Rights? (Select all that apply)
opts: They are justiciable in nature, meaning they are enforceable by courts.
They are not sacrosanct or permanent and can be curtailed by Parliament via Article 368.
They are absolute and cannot be subjected to any state restrictions.
During a National Emergency, all Fundamental Rights are suspended automatically.
masteryZone.sol: Fundamental Rights are justiciable (enforceable) and can be amended by Parliament under Article 368 (without altering basic structure). They are not absolute (qualified) and not all are automatically suspended (Articles 20 and 21 are never suspended).

masteryZone.q: True or False: Fundamental Rights are only available against the actions of the State and never against private individuals.
masteryZone.sol: False. While most rights are available against the State, some rights (like Articles 17, 23, and 24) are also enforceable against private individuals.

masteryZone.q: Fill in the blank: The Fundamental Rights are intended to promote the ideal of ________ democracy.
masteryZone.sol: Fundamental Rights promote the ideal of political democracy, whereas DPSPs promote social and economic democracy.

masteryZone.q: Match the following Fundamental Rights categories with their corresponding article range:
masteryZone.sol: Equality corresponds to 14-18, Freedom corresponds to 19-22, and Against Exploitation corresponds to 23-24.

masteryZone.q: List the article numbers of the Fundamental Rights that are available exclusively to citizens of India.
masteryZone.sol: Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, and 30.

masteryZone.q:
Assertion (A): Fundamental Rights are described as justiciable in nature.
Reason (R): A person can directly approach the Supreme Court of India under Article 32 if any of their Fundamental Rights are violated.
Select the correct code:
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
masteryZone.sol: Justiciable means enforceable in a court of law. Approachability under Article 32 directly to the Supreme Court confirms and explains this justiciability.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the suspension of Article 19:
Statement I: Article 19 is automatically suspended when a National Emergency is declared on the grounds of armed rebellion.
Statement II: Laws made during such an emergency cannot be challenged even after the emergency expires.
Which of the following is correct?
opts: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement II is correct but Statement I is incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are incorrect. Article 19 is only suspended during external emergencies (war/aggression), not internal (armed rebellion). Laws made during emergency can be challenged for inconsistency after the emergency expires, except for actions taken during the emergency.

masteryZone.q: Why are Fundamental Rights in India not considered absolute?
masteryZone.sol: Because the Constitution strikes a balance between individual liberty and social control. The State can impose reasonable restrictions on these rights to protect public order, morality, security, and sovereignty of India.

masteryZone.q: How can the classification of Fundamental Rights be altered by the Parliament?
masteryZone.sol: Parliament can add, delete, or modify classifications by passing a constitutional amendment act under Article 368 with a special majority, provided it does not alter the Basic Structure of the Constitution (such as when Article 31 was deleted).

masteryZone.q: A foreign tourist visiting India wants to set up a permanent trade shop in New Delhi. When denied permission by the local municipality, the tourist claims a violation of Article 19(1)(g) (freedom of trade and profession). Assess the tourist's claim.
masteryZone.sol: The tourist's claim is invalid. Article 19 (which includes the freedom to practice any profession or carry on any occupation, trade, or business) is exclusive to citizens of India and is not available to foreigners.

masteryZone.q: Explain the concept of 'Justiciability' and how it sets Fundamental Rights apart from other rights in the Constitution.
masteryZone.sol: Justiciability means that if a right is violated, the aggrieved party has the legal authority to approach the courts for direct enforcement. Unlike Directive Principles (Part IV) which are non-justiciable and require legislative action to execute, Fundamental Rights (Part III) are directly enforceable. Under Article 32, a person can approach the Supreme Court directly, making the court a guarantor and defender of these rights.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following is NOT covered under the definition of 'State' in Article 12?
opts: The Delhi Municipal Corporation
The Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL)
The Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI)
The Legislative Assembly of Rajasthan
masteryZone.sol: The Supreme Court in the Zee Telefilms case ruled that BCCI is not a 'State' because it is not functionally, financially, or administratively dominated or controlled by the government.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following doctrines are derived from or associated with Article 13? (Select all that apply)
opts: Doctrine of Eclipse
Doctrine of Severability
Doctrine of Waiver
Doctrine of Pith and Substance
masteryZone.sol: Eclipse, Severability, and Waiver are directly associated with Article 13. Pith and Substance is used to resolve legislative competence disputes under Article 246 (relations between Union and States).

masteryZone.q: True or False: Under the Doctrine of Waiver, a citizen can choose to waive off their Fundamental Rights if it is done voluntarily.
masteryZone.sol: False. In India, a person cannot waive off or surrender their Fundamental Rights because they are established as a matter of public policy and are mandatory protections.

masteryZone.q: Fill in the blank: Pre-constitutional laws violating Fundamental Rights do not become void ab initio but are overshadowed under the Doctrine of ________.
masteryZone.sol: The Doctrine of Eclipse states that pre-constitutional laws violating FRs are not dead but eclipsed (dormant) and can be revived if the constitutional restriction is removed.

masteryZone.q: Match the judicial doctrine with its core meaning under Article 13:

options.text: Only invalid portions of law are struck down

masteryZone.sol: Severability matches invalid portions, Eclipse matches dormancy, and Waiver matches inability to surrender rights.

masteryZone.q: What is the status of a post-constitutional law that violates a Fundamental Right from the moment of its enactment?
masteryZone.sol: It is void ab initio (void from the very beginning) to the extent of its inconsistency.

masteryZone.q:
Assertion (A): The judiciary, when performing administrative functions, is considered 'State' under Article 12.
Reason (R): The definition of State under Article 12 includes all authorities under the control of the Government of India.
Select the correct code:
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are true. Because 'State' covers all authorities under government control, when the judiciary acts administratively (like making appointments), it operates as an administrative authority and falls under Article 12.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the definition of 'Law' under Article 13:
Statement I: Executive orders and notifications issued by administrative authorities are considered 'law'.
Statement II: Custom and usage having the force of law are excluded from the scope of Article 13.
Which of the following is correct?
opts: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement II is correct but Statement I is incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
masteryZone.sol: Statement I is correct. Statement II is incorrect because custom or usage having the force of law is explicitly included under Article 13(3)(a).

masteryZone.q: Why is the definition of State under Article 12 made so broad?
masteryZone.sol: To ensure that all public authorities, local bodies, and government agencies that have the capacity to violate individual rights are bound by the disciplines of Part III, thereby preventing state agencies from bypassing constitutional checks.

masteryZone.q: How does the Doctrine of Eclipse apply to post-constitutional laws in India?
masteryZone.sol: While the doctrine primarily applies to pre-constitutional laws, courts have held that if a constitutional amendment removes the clash between a post-constitutional law and a Fundamental Right, that law can also be revived, provided it did not involve lack of legislative competence.

masteryZone.q: A state legislature passes an education act. Section 4 of this act violates the right to equality under Article 14. The rest of the act is completely valid and can function independently. Determine what action the High Court should take under Article 13.
masteryZone.sol: Applying the Doctrine of Severability, the High Court should declare only Section 4 of the education act unconstitutional and void, while keeping the rest of the act operational, as it can survive independently.

masteryZone.q: Explain the difference between a pre-constitutional law and a post-constitutional law in relation to Article 13.
masteryZone.sol: Under Article 13(1), pre-constitutional laws (laws in force before Jan 26, 1950) that violate FRs are not void from inception (void ab initio) but only become inoperative to the extent of their inconsistency (Doctrine of Eclipse). Under Article 13(2), post-constitutional laws (laws made after Jan 26, 1950) that violate FRs are void ab initio (void from their very birth) because the State is forbidden from making such laws.

sections.title: 3. Evolution, Importance & Constitutional Safeguards of Part III

masteryZone.q: Which of the following is correct regarding the I.R. Coelho Case (2007) and the Ninth Schedule?
opts: The Ninth Schedule was declared completely unconstitutional.
Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule are subject to basic structure review if added after April 24, 1973.
Parliament can no longer add laws to the Ninth Schedule.
All laws in the Ninth Schedule are immune to judicial review.
masteryZone.sol: In the I.R. Coelho case (2007), the Supreme Court ruled that laws added to the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973, can be challenged if they violate the Basic Structure.

masteryZone.q: Which of the following articles restrict or limit the application of Fundamental Rights? (Select all that apply)
opts: Article 31A
Article 31C
Article 33
Article 35
masteryZone.sol: Articles 31A, 31C, 33, and 34 limit or restrict the scope of rights. Article 35 is enabling, granting legislative authority on rights exclusively to the Parliament.

masteryZone.q: True or False: Under Article 34, martial law can only be declared when a National Emergency is in force.
masteryZone.sol: False. Martial law under Article 34 is distinct from National Emergency and can be declared in any area where military rule is necessary to restore order, independent of a countrywide emergency.

masteryZone.q: Fill in the blank: Article 31B protects laws listed in the ________ Schedule of the Constitution from being challenged.
masteryZone.sol: Article 31B protects laws placed in the Ninth Schedule.

masteryZone.q: Match the Article with its corresponding scope of safeguard or restriction:

options.text: Restricts lawmaking power on rights to Parliament

masteryZone.sol: Article 33 matches Armed Forces, Article 34 matches Martial Law, and Article 35 matches Parliament's exclusive power.

masteryZone.q: Which article protects laws giving effect to directive principles in Article 39(b) and 39(c)?
masteryZone.sol: Article 31C.

masteryZone.q:
Assertion (A): State Legislatures cannot pass laws prescribing punishment for untouchability.
Reason (R): Article 35 vests the power to legislate on offenses under Part III exclusively in the Parliament to maintain uniformity.
Select the correct code:
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
masteryZone.sol: Both statements are true. Parliament has the exclusive power under Article 35, which explains why state legislatures are barred from passing such laws.

masteryZone.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the Ninth Schedule:
Statement I: The Ninth Schedule was added to the Constitution by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act.
Statement II: The date April 24, 1973, is significant because it represents the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment.
Which of the following is correct?
opts: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement II is correct but Statement I is incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
masteryZone.sol: Statement I is incorrect because the Ninth Schedule was added by the First Amendment Act in 1951. Statement II is correct.

masteryZone.q: Why did the farmers of the Constitution exclude State Legislatures from legislating on Fundamental Rights under Article 35?
masteryZone.sol: To ensure that the application, protection, and penalties for violating Fundamental Rights remain completely uniform throughout the territory of India, preventing regional disparities.

masteryZone.q: How does Article 31C protect certain laws from being struck down under Article 14 and 19?
masteryZone.sol: Article 31C declares that no law that seeks to give effect to the directive principles in Article 39(b) and 39(c) can be declared void on the ground that it is inconsistent with Article 14 or Article 19.

masteryZone.q: An officer in the Indian Army publishes a book criticizing government defense policies without obtaining permission. When court-martialed, he claims a violation of his freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a). Evaluate this defense.
masteryZone.sol: The defense is invalid. Under Article 33, Parliament has enacted military laws (such as the Army Act) that abridge or restrict the fundamental rights of armed forces members, including freedom of speech, to maintain strict discipline.

masteryZone.q: Explain the significance of the Ninth Schedule and how the I.R. Coelho Case restored the balance of judicial review.
masteryZone.sol: The Ninth Schedule was created to protect land reform laws from judicial scrutiny. Over time, governments used it to shield controversial laws. In the I.R. Coelho case (2007), the Supreme Court ruled that judicial review is a basic feature. While the schedule itself remains, any law placed in it after April 24, 1973, is open to challenge if it violates the Basic Structure of the Constitution. This restored the balance by preventing the creation of a 'constitutional black hole' immune to judicial review.
